Case study 02

Afromerica Entertainment

A competition and events platform with paid voting, live results and ticket checkout.

Year
2025
Work
Sole developer · Engineering, Implementation
Tools
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase (Postgres, Auth, Realtime), Paystack, Resend, Sentry, Tailwind, Vercel
Afromerica cover — real screenshot

Overview

A competition and events platform I built end to end — from the database and APIs to the admin dashboard — with paid voting, a live judged finale, and ticket checkout. Scoring is computed in the database so the leaderboard stays correct under load.

Why this work mattered

A live competition needs voting people trust and a finale that can be scored in real time, in front of an audience. The platform had to take money, count votes and show results without going down at the worst possible moment.

What I needed to solve

Paid votes and public votes had to combine with judges’ scores and performance into one final result, on a fixed weighting, with no double-counting and no way to tamper with the tally. Payments had to be idempotent, and the leaderboard had to update live.

Definition of done: votes, tickets and scores reconcile to the same number every time; a dropped or repeated webhook never changes the tally; results update in real time.

How I approached it

I put the scoring logic in the database rather than the app, so the final weighting is computed once from the source rows. Payment webhooks are signed and idempotent, so a retry can’t inflate a count. Realtime subscriptions push leaderboard changes to the client.

Architecture diagram — light / dark

Fig 1. Paystack webhook → signed, idempotent handler → Postgres scoring → realtime leaderboard. Your existing light/dark architecture SVG slots in here.

What I delivered

Paid voting with a live leaderboard, an event-management dashboard, and ticket checkout with Paystack, on REST APIs over Postgres with signed, idempotent payment webhooks and realtime updates.

MeasureValue
Final weighting (paid / public / judges / performance)35 / 10 / 30 / 25
API routes23
One-time-code expiry10 min

Result & handoff

The platform ran the finale with voting, ticketing and live results. Performance was tracked with Lighthouse and Core Web Vitals, and errors routed to Sentry.

The person behind the work

About

I came to software through engineering, hospitality and hands-on systems work. That mix taught me to listen first, make the complicated clear and stay with a problem until it works.

Bio

I’m Daniel Akoko, though most people call me Tobi. I’m a software engineer in Dallas, Texas. I build web software for churches and small businesses, and I pay close attention to the parts people usually notice only when they fail: the information on the page, the error message after a wrong turn, the test that catches a regression and the documentation someone needs after handover.

My route into software was not a straight line. I studied electrical engineering, then criminology, then computer science. I worked in hospitality, where I learned to stay calm when the room is busy and take care of the person in front of me. For years I have also run sound, media and livestreaming at church.

That mix shapes how I work now. I listen before I propose, turn complicated work into clear steps and stay with a project through testing, launch and handover. The goal is not simply to ship software. It is to leave people with something they can understand, use and depend on.
